newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - TI to focus on new chips - CFO.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - TI to focus on new chips - CFO.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc expects continued volatility in the troubled market for memory chips and plans to focus on higher-margin digital signal processors in its search for stronger profits, Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said.
"We need to focus more on our objectives and our focus of DSPS (digital signal processing solutions)," Aylesworth told Reuters in a telephone interview.
He said the key market for memory chips would remain volatile at least in the short-term because of excess supply.
"Bit growth is strong but prices continue to decline rapidly as well. We expect a difficult market environment in the near-term," Aylesworth

He said memory chip inventories held by customers were at low levels but that excessive industry-wide production, which caused an 80 percent drop in prices in 1996, remains a problem and that it is not clear when the market will straighten out.
"We don't have a view as to what time there will be better balance there," he said.

TI earlier reported a net loss of $0.15 per share in the fourth quarter, compared to a profit of $1.50 in the same period of 1995. The First Call consensus of analysts' estimates had predicted a profit of $0.68 for the quarter.

But Aylesworth said the net result was hit by one-time special charges such as $91 million of severance costs related to a voluntary retirement plan and $117 million of asset write-downs on certain product lines in the mobile computing unit as well as a $15 million additional tax provision.
"Taking that all into account .... we were reasonably in line with expectations for the business on an ongoing basis."
The company said net income from continuing operations, excluding the fourth quarter special charges, was $0.50.
Aylesworth said the bright spot in the earnings report was again provided by digital signal processing solutions.

He said orders for the products, which convert sights and sounds into digital computer language, were 30 percent higher than in the last three months of 1995 and predicted strong growth in 1997. "We see every indication that the trend of strong revenue growth is going to continue."

When asked if the company could continue to grow DSPS revenues by 30 percent per year, Aylesworth said: "That is certainly not out of the question. We don't have a specific forecast but that kind of trend line growth over a period of time is certainly possible."

The company also said earlier that it was selling its mobile computing business to Taiwan-based Acer Inc, but did not disclose terms. The announcement followed the sale earlier this month of TI's defense unit to Raytheon Co for $2.95 billion, and fits in with a strategic shift towards DSPS.
Aylesworth said the mobile computing unit had seen strong revenue growth but that TI wanted to concentrate on DSPS.

"We decided the mobile computing business itself could be a greater success by being part of a company with a more complete line of computer products," he said. "Even though the team had grown revenues very significantly over the past couple of years, they were really at a disadvantage of not being part of a complete-line computer company."
He declined to detail the mobile computing unit's revenues in 1996 but said they accounted for "something under half" the $1.7 billion of revenues in TI's digital products division.

Aylesworth said the "vast majority" of the $1.1 billion set aside for capital spending in 1997 would go to supporting capacity expansion in the DSPS business, which has displaced memory chips as the largest single source of revenues and accounted for about 40 percent of $8.1 billion in total semiconductor revenues last year.

"The centerpiece and focus of our direction is DSPS," Aylesworth said. He said proceeds from the sale of the defense and mobile computing units would go to reinvestment in growth businesses and that reducing debt is of "secondary importance".
